News.title: Terrifying moment 300kg grizzly bear circles hiker walking her dog before charging at brave woman screaming ‘get away’
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment a 300kg grizzly bear circles a hiker as she walks her dog.

Horrifying footage shows the huge beast charging at the woman and her pooch in a dramatic stand off, as she yells “get away”.





The woman was out walking her dog in Alberta, Canada, when the predator approached.

Video shows the bear prowling towards the hiker and her dog, but she bravely stands firm.

The woman can be heard shouting “no”, “get away” as her petrified pet stands rooted to the ground.

She then makes strange animal noises to try and scare off the beast.

Her dog faces off with the bear, slowly backing away as the predator inches closer.

The grizzly bear wanders closer before suddenly charging towards the woman and her pooch.



It chases the dog, pausing to stand on its hind legs menacingly, before continuing its pursuit.

The bear then bounds away and the hiker and her dog breathe a sigh of relief.

It retreats behind a gate and the hiker takes her chance to flee.



Experts say running is the worst thing to do when approached by a grizzly bear.

This can trigger their chase instinct – and they’re much faster than humans.

The woman backed away slowly initially instead of making a run for it.

Alberta Parks officials said: “Safety of visitors is always our top priority, and staff are monitoring the situation closely.”

They advise visitors to make loud noises and travel in groups to avoid close calls with the creatures.



Walkers should keep their dogs on leads and keep an eye out for signs the beasts have been around recently.

These include fresh digging or scat.

If a bear does approach, visitors are advised to stand their ground, and speak in a low, calm voice.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They should never scream or climb a tree to escape.

News.title: ‘Explosion’ heard as fire engine bursts into flames en route to serious crash and billows of smoke fill sky
News.content:
ENGINE INFERNO ‘Explosion’ heard as fire engine bursts into flames en route to serious crash and billows of smoke fill sky

A FIRE engine has burst into flames while en route to a road collision – with “explosions” being heard from the blazing inferno.

Emergency crews rushed to the burning vehicle on the A350 at Charlton Marshall in Dorset.





Firefighters battled to put out the fire with three hose reel jets while the vehicle’s tyres and equipment on board exploded.

One local said: “I heard sirens and a screech of tyres outside and came out of my house to see thick black smoke.

“I could see one firefighter up the road running down towards me saying telling me to go inside as there were oxygen tanks on board and it was going to blow.

“There were then a series of loud explosions with the roof of the cab of the truck blowing off into the air and landing on the pavement.”

Another resident added: “There were maybe three or four subsequent explosions and the electricity lines above the engine started to go up in flames too.

“About 20 minutes later, back up fire engines arrived and attempted to extinguish the fire.”



The crew from Blandford fire station was driving down the A-road in response to a traffic incident on June 24.

At 6.24pm, a fire erupted in the vehicle, with the driver able to stop safely.

Firefighters from Wimborne and Sturminster Newton were mobilised to the scene.

A pair of breathing apparatus wearers and multiple hose reel jets were used to put out the fire.

Locals said they could hear explosions from the fire, which were the vehicle’s tyres and cylinders onboard exploding.



The fire from the vehicle had destroyed the cab, with damage done to the nearby grass verge and telegraph cables.

Paramedics tended to the crew from the burning fire engine, with emergency personnel closing off the road.

An investigation into the incident has been launched to find out how the vehicle caught fire.

A Dorset and Wiltshire Fire and Rescue spokesperson said: “A crew from Blandford fire station was making an emergency response to a road traffic collision at 6.24pm last night (24 June) when a fire started in the fire engine while they were travelling on the A350 at Charlton Marshall.

“The crew was able to stop safely, and no-one was injured. Crews from Wimborne and Sturminster Newton were mobilised to deal with the fire, and two breathing apparatus wearers and three hose reel jets were used.



“Local residents would have heard explosions, which were the vehicle’s tyres and also cylinders on board, including breathing apparatus sets.

“An investigation into how the fire started is now underway.

“The stop came in at 8.22pm, the vehicle cab has been destroyed by fire and there was damage to the adjacent grass verge and telegraph cables.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The firefighters involved have been checked over as a precaution by paramedics, with no issues.

“The road will remain closed for some time to allow for vehicle recovery; the carriageway may need repairs, so drivers should check their route before setting off in the morning.”

News.title: Zoo where boy, 3, was ‘thrown into crocodile pit by man with learning difficulties’ reopens nine days after terror
News.content:
CROC HORROR Zoo where boy, 3, was ‘thrown into crocodile pit by man with learning difficulties’ reopens nine days after terror

Credit: Reuters

THE ZOO where a three-year-old boy was tossed into the crocodile pit has announced it is reopening after the shocking incident.

Johnsons of Old Hurst said its whole site will be open “as of this weekend”, after the boy was left in critical condition.





In a social media post today, Johnsons of Old Hurst said: “As of this weekend, our whole site will be fully open, thank you.”

It comes after the small child was allegedly thrown 15 ft into the crocodile enclosure by a man with learning difficulties last Thursday.

The boy landed on a concrete walkway, resulting in a broken arm and pelvis — and then ended up in the water.

It’s believed that the boy had been bitten by one of the crocs – either a saltwater or Nile crocodile.

He was raced to hospital with serious injuries and was in critical but stable condition.

Now, the zoo and farm where the shocking incident occurred has announced it is reopening its doors.



The 30-year-old suspect was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder but swiftly release from police custody.

Cops confirmed the man was not fit to be quizzed by officers and he has been bailed until September 18.

The announcement comes after the zoo initially said the Tropical House would be “closed until further notice” in a social media post last week.

Its statement read: “Our thoughts and prayers are with the boy and his family following the incident that occurred today.

“Out of respect to the family, our Tropical House will remain closed until further notice.”



The Johnsons added: “The rest of the site will remain open as usual.”

Yesterday, it emerged that the suspect was reportedly bundled into a car by his carers moments after the horror.

Police are now reportedly probing the two carers who were looking after the suspect during his trip to the zoo.

A source told The Telegraph that the suspect and carers left the enclosure and went to the car park after the child was thrown into the pit.

They then tried to get into a vehicle but did not leave the zoo grounds after employees intervened.



The source said: “They tried to get him into the car”.

But “another member of staff was there and prevented them from leaving” they added.

This follows reports that the carers were on their phones as the trio made their way around the zoo.

A mum, in her 20s, said: “Someone later described the man that did it and said he was with carers.

“I don’t know if it was definitely him but I saw one bloke of a bigger build, he had two carers with him and they weren’t paying him much attention.



“If it was him, his carers were maybe ten metres behind him and not paying much attention.

“They were English and chatting among themselves and on their phones.”

Cambridgeshire Police is reportedly reviewing CCTV of the incident to decide if any further action should be taken.

Tracey Johnson, who co-owns and runs the zoo, was one of the first to jump in after the child.

Her husband, Andrew clambered in after her, along with their son Edward.



The three of them bravely rescued the child, and prised him away from the grip of one of the beasts.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Cops are currently assessing the role of the carers who were meant to be supervising the vulnerable adult during the outing.

As of Monday, the child is no longer in critical condition.

News.title: Woman who waged 15-yr war against neighbours hit with restraining order after spying & throwing dead moles over fence
News.content:
NEIGHBOUR HELL Woman who waged 15-yr war against neighbours hit with restraining order after spying & throwing dead moles over fence

A NIGHTMARE neighbour who waged a 15-year war against the couple next door has been hit with a restraining order.

Pensioner Zoi Hayes has already been hauled before the courts more than once over the bitter feud with her long-suffering neighbours Peter and Corrine Rotherham.





The pair have lived next door to each other in the Wiltshire village of Urchfont since the Rotherham’s moved into their bungalow in 2011.

The row has featured claims of spying through a hole cut in a hedge, throwing dead moles over a fence and banging a wheelie bin before dawn.

The latest clash unfolded when Hayes deliberately left a lawnmower running beside the couple’s garden while they hosted friends for a summer tapas party, a court heard.

Guests became so frustrated by the noise they went next door to ask her to switch it off.



But prosecutors said she had deliberately left the mower running to “annoy” Mrs Rotherham, putting her in breach of an existing restraining order.

Salisbury Magistrates’ Court heard the couple were entertaining six friends at a tapas party on a sunny July evening when the drama unfolded.



Prosecutor Robert Salamé said: “It was a sunny evening and at around 7.30pm the defendant parked her lawnmower directly next to the fence and she left the engine running loudly for approximately an hour.”

“It caused Corrine a degree of distress and her friends went next door to speak to Zoi.

“She admitted doing it to annoy Corrine and the matter was subsequently reported to the police as this amounted to a breach of the restraining order conditions.”

Secret footage of the incident was later used as part of a police investigation.

The latest court appearance is far from the first chapter in the remarkable neighbour war.



In 2021 Hayes was handed a five-year restraining order after damaging one of Mrs Rotherham’s sweet pea flowers.

She later breached that order and received a six-week prison sentence suspended for 12 months.

The court heard there was a “lengthy history of disputes” between the neighbours stretching back around 15 years.

Hayes admitted harassment which breached the restraining order.

She was fined £348 and ordered to pay a £139 victim surcharge and £85 in court costs.



Magistrates also imposed a fresh two-year restraining order banning her from contacting the couple or visiting their home.

The court heard Hayes has since moved from Urchfont to Dorset.

But in a statement read to the court, Mrs Rotherham said she feared Hayes could return to the area.

She said: “My concern is that she will come back to the area as she has never accepted that she has done anything wrong.

“I have heard that she is obsessed with getting revenge.”



Mrs Rotherham has previously described Hayes as a “neighbour from hell” after years of alleged harassment.

She said: “It was like living with a Peeping Tom who was absolutely obsessed with you. She cut a hole in the hedge so she could look through so we had to grow it out.

“We avoided her like the plague. It was just hell. She was a compulsive liar and a neighbour from hell.”

Representing herself, she apologised for the lawnmower incident.

Hayes said: “I would like to begin by expressing my sincere remorse for my actions and I deeply regret that incident.



“I understand that what I did was wrong and I am sorry.”

Sentencing, magistrates’ chairman Timothy Watts said: “We have listened carefully to your evidence and the prosecution.

“We noted your remorse but we also noted your relevant convictions.

“We have decided to deal with this with a fine. A restraining order will be put in place for two years.”

But after sentence was passed, Hayes launched one final broadside at her long-time rival.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

She said: “You have to remember that there are two sides to every story.

“She finds a way to twist everything. I will only be happy when she takes her last breath.”

News.title: Home Secretary blasted over new ‘open borders’ scheme to allow thousands of refugees into UK legally
News.content:
NEW ROUTES Home Secretary blasted over new ‘open borders’ scheme to allow thousands of refugees into UK legally

Credit: PA

THOUSANDS of refugees will be brought to the UK under a new scheme set to be launched by the Home Secretary next week.

Political opponents slammed the Government for the “open borders” plan, arguing there needs to be a crackdown on illegal immigration first.





Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce “capped safe and legal” routes to the UK in a bid to crack down on small boat migrants.

Applications for the new community sponsorship scheme will open this autumn, according to The Times.

More than 10,000 refugees are hoped to be brought into the country in the next decade under the new resettlement scheme.

Tory shadow home secretary Chris Philp blasted the plans, arguing “it won’t stop the boats”.



Philp said: “75,000 illegal immigrants have entered the UK in the last two years.

“Until this is zero, we shouldn’t be shipping any extra people in at all on ‘humanitarian’ grounds.



“Unless every person that wants to come is let in (which would be mad) it won’t stop the boats.

“Open borders Labour revealing their true colours again.”

So far this year, more than 11,000 migrants have crossed the Channel in small boats.

The figure for 2026 so far is almost 40 per cent down compared to this time last year.

The Liberal Democrats also agreed more needed to be done to stop small boat arrivals.



But Max Wilkinson, Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesman, said the new scheme was a “step in the right direction”.

Mahmood said the new route would allow in “genuine refugees” and “close loopholes that have too often been abused”.

It will allow universities and other approved organisations to “sponsor” refugees to come and live in the UK after undergoing background checks.

“Britain has always offered sanctuary to those fleeing war and persecution,” Mahmood told the BBC.

Due to be announced in the government’s Immigration and Asylum Bill on Tuesday, it is regarded as an attempt by Mahmood to win over the left flank of the Labour Party.



The bill also contains controversial legislation cracking down on the asylum appeal system.

This includes reforms to human rights and modern slavery laws to make it easier for the Home Office to reject “vexatious” asylum claims.

She has already ended permanent refugee status, replacing it with temporary protections.

While the Home Secretary is expected to keep her job if Burnham becomes leader, she has faced criticism within the party for her strict asylum policies.

The new route is intended to help refugees who are fleeing conflict and natural disasters in their home country.



Another route, which would allow refugees to be sponsored by employers, is set to be rolled out next year.

It is thought the Home Office will cap the number of arrivals under the scheme, but it is not known how many that might be.

The reforms are understood to be based on the Canadian scheme, which allows people to “sponsor” refugees by pledging to provide support, including finances, for a year after they arrive.

This is similar to the Homes for Ukraine scheme which saw 200,000 Ukrainians sponsored to come to the UK on temporary visas.

While this was seen as a successful project, the Home Secretary reportedly hopes her new scheme will replace these “ad hoc” programmes for specific countries.



It comes as the Home Office has sunk into all-out farce with Mahmood banning her own immigration minister from viewing official documents.

She imposed the extraordinary restriction on Mike Tapp after Starmer refused to fire him for writing an article in The Times to publicly argue foreign care workers should be spared Labour’s tougher settlement rules.

He wrote it was his “strong belief” foreign care workers who had “played by the rules” should not face Labour’s planned extension of the wait for indefinite leave to remain from five years to ten.

He will stay in post but cannot view Home Office papers or hold official meetings without approval.

Mahmood was unaware of the article before it was published and asked Sir Keir to sack him for a Ministerial Code breach.



But No 10 made it clear that the final decision rested with the PM.

A spokesman said: “It is not for any individual Secretary of State to determine whether the Ministerial Code has been followed, it is a matter for the PM alone.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Earlier, Tapp insisted on social media: “I won’t be intimidated to drop my views. Stay classy!”

The row triggered a backlash inside Labour, with one Government aide branding Mahmood “completely shameless and dishonourable”.

News.title: Incredible moment South Korea uses LASER CANNONS to shoot down 50-drone swarm in live military drills
News.content:
THIS is the astonishing moment South Korea uses laser cannons to shoot down a swarm of 50 drones during a live-fire drill.

Incredible footage shows eight Vulcan guns shooting barrage fire to counter a throng of infiltrating drones.





The mass of unmanned aircraft is obliterated as it approaches the weapons.

Within seconds dozens of drones are shot out of the sky leaving only six in flight.

The remaining six were then destroyed at close range with one portable laser and five shotguns.

“This was the first drill to defend against the infiltration of drone swarms, which are emerging as a powerful threat, using existing assets such as Vulcan guns,” said Colonel Nam Hyung-joo, head of the information operations division at the Missile Defense Command.



“Based on the results and lessons from this exercise, we will continue to develop our drone swarm response system”, he added.

It comes as South Korea‘s defence minister announced a sweeping overall of its warfare strategy that will see all military forces trained as drone operators.



Ahn Gyu-back said: “All soldiers should be able to use drones like a second personal firearm.”

Around 500,000 military personnel will be trained to become “drone warriors”, the ministry added.

Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have seen the rapid advancement of drone warfare.



Drones are now a “gamechanger” on the battle field and have “fundamentally changed the nature of warfare”, Ahn said.

The military plans to bolster its forces with about 11,000 commercial drones by the end of this year.

This will increase its total to 60,000 alongside 20,000 low-cost disposable drones by 2030.

At the same time, South Korea is expanding its counter drone systems with laser weapons.

Plans to strengthen its air power capabilities comes after five small North Korean drones breached South Korean airspace in 2022.



One even entered the no-fly zone above the presidential office in a huge blow to Seoul’s security forces.

The military deployed jets in a desperate bid to counter the threat and fired around 100 shots but failed to down a single drone.

It comes as North Korea’s military partnership with Russia deepens, giving its military direct exposure to drone warfare in action.

Kim Jong-un has previously sent tens of thousands of workers overseas to replace Russians killed or wounded in the invasion of Ukraine.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Between 2,000 and 3,000 North Koreans are believed to have been killed in the war, South Korean intelligence states.



And speculation is swirling that a new influx of war fighters are on their way from North Korea to Russia under a pact sealed by the Putin regime.

News.title: I stood by my husband after he spent hours watching child sex abuse online – it nearly killed him but he’s no paedophile
News.content:
CROUCHED over his computer for hours on end, Paul Gullon-Scott had become a shadow of his former self.

Watching hours of sickening child abuse images and extreme violence, left loving wife Fiona unable to recognise the man her husband had become. But this was not some predator examining the most chilling content imaginable.





Dad-of-two Paul spent 14 years as a digital forensic investigator with Northumbria Police force, where he sifted through countless disturbing images and videos documenting the abuse of innocent children, each case leaving its own mark and some leaving lasting scars.

Unable to speak about his work, he also wanted to protect his family by not contaminating the minds of the people he loved most with pictures they had never asked to see.

In a brutally honest account, Paul and Fiona – who are raising awareness of the urgent need for better support for those repeatedly exposed to trauma – bravely open up about how the job led him to the depths of despair and nearly drove him to the brink of suicide.

When Paul first applied to the unit, their bread and butter was mainly fraud, murder and drugs. But as time went on, the content became much more harrowing.

Speaking to The Sun, he says: “There is no way you can possibly prepare yourself for what you’re going to be exposed to in that role, the depravity of the material that you are openly exposed to, Stephen King couldn’t write it.”

The team’s office had a warning on the always-locked door: ‘Explicit material on show behind this door”, as investigators spent day after day, hour after hour, watching, listening and reading distressing evidence in the hope of being able to identify the child victim to ensure their future safety.

Fiona, 54, says: “Paul was always someone who believed that strength came from containing emotions and shielding our family from the horrors he saw daily at work.

“He never spoke about what he had seen at work, pushing that deep inside. ‘Support’ at work was an annual 10-minute chat with Occupational Health, resulting in a couple of sentences stating he was fit to work. It was laughable.





“I knew different. He was becoming more and more irritable, less able to sleep, and increasingly building a wall around himself. He started smoking more and more, losing weight and looking gaunt and haggard.

“With friends and wider family, he would put on an act of being ‘normal’, but even that started to slip, and those who had only seen him as caring, kind and full of life, started to see more and more glimpses of negativity, grouchiness and disengagement.”

Fiona says that Paul began to drink more each weekend, later learning it was a means to escape reliving the nightmares of what he had seen at work and finally sleep.

She says: “I cycled between feeling concerned for him, to feeling angry that he was drinking to the point he couldn’t walk straight, to feeling pity for a man who was always so strong and now seemed broken and beaten.”

Paul, 55, was not allowed to talk about the cases that he was investigating – but neither did he want to.

Close to tears, he says: “How do you explain to your partner that you have just spent eight hours examining videos depicting babies being abused? How can that sit alongside a family meal or a normal evening at home.

“Part of my silence was professional obligation, part was self-preservation. And part of it was fear, fear that if I described even a fraction of what I had seen, I would transfer those images into the minds of my family.

“But while I thought my silence protected them, instead they felt the after-effects: the quietness, the distance, the reduced emotional connection.”



The stress of the job led to Paul drinking to excess, and on occasion, the hours of horror he was forced to watch would spill out.

Fiona says: “He would tell me things he had had to watch and listen to at work. Things he – in sober daytime – insisted he would never share because they were just too awful, describing the sounds, the screams, the images.

“Sometimes he would break down and cry uncontrollably, voicing things I could not understand and speaking of ‘the pink baby’ through wracking sobs and heaving gasps for air. I saw Paul had this almost obsession with identifying that child to save her.”

At one of Paul’s lowest points, after an argument with Fiona over nothing, he stormed out of the house.

Fiona says: “He was in such a state of distress and turmoil, I was intensely worried for him. He had turned off his ‘find my friends’, ignored all my calls, and I had no idea where he was or what he was doing.

“In desperation, I rang one of his best friends, who called him and managed to get through and was able to reassure me he was just getting some headspace.

“I recently found out he had, in fact, driven to a local bridge and was contemplating taking his life. Whatever it was that stopped him from doing so, I will be eternally grateful.”

Concerned, Fiona and Paul’s friends tried to speak to him on several occasions, but Paul continued to go to work day after day.

How to get help EVERY 90 minutes in the UK a life is lost to suicide It doesn’t discriminate, touching the lives of people in every corner of society – from the homeless and unemployed to builders and doctors, reality stars and footballers. It’s the biggest killer of people under the age of 35, more deadly than cancer and car crashes. And men are three times more likely to take their own life than women. Yet it’s rarely spoken of, a taboo that threatens to continue its deadly rampage unless we all stop and take notice, now. If you, or anyone you know, needs help dealing with mental health problems, the following organisations provide support: CALM, www.thecalmzone.net, 0800 585 858

Heads Together,www.headstogether.org.uk

HUMEN www.wearehumen.org

Mind, www.mind.org.uk, 0300 123 3393

Papyrus, www.papyrus-uk.org, 0800 068 41 41

Samaritans,www.samaritans.org, 116 123

She says: “He would argue that if he didn’t, then who would save the children being abused. He felt this intense responsibility to save these children, and if he left, he would be letting them down.



“Day after day, he would come home a shell of who he used to be”.

Family life became increasingly fraught, as Paul retreated further from his family, thinking he was protecting them.

Paul says: “Hypervigilance served me well in forensic examinations, but it is not a tool you can just switch off.

“I would find myself scanning environments, noticing exits, observing who was nearby, assessing risk in situations that did not require assessment, and never sitting with my back to the room.

“It felt like I was holding my breath, waiting for something to happen.”

Paul’s work also affected the way he parented.

He says: “Working in CSAM (Child Sex Abuse Material) investigations changes how you see the world. I became intensely aware of online risks.

“When you repeatedly witness the worst outcomes of digital harm, the line between professional fear and personal fear can become blurred.”

After working on tens of thousands of cases, Paul was close to breaking point.

He says: “The day I realised I could not do this job anymore, I could barely function. When I stepped through the front door, I looked at my wife, unable to hold back the tears.



“The only words I could manage were ‘I am broken. I can’t do this anymore’. Those words were met with love, and Fiona wrapped her arms around me and quietly said, ‘You have done your duty. Don’t go back; we’ll be fine.”

Fiona adds: “I could see the immense effort it took him to say he needed help, I could see he thought it made him weak, that he wasn’t being a man. He was utterly broken, but we were all so proud of him. It took immense strength to admit.”

At first, Paul went to a counsellor through the Employee Assist Programme but found it unsuccessful, and the couple forked out for private therapy.

Fiona says: “It took 13 months, but the difference was immense. I got my husband back; he was lighter in spirit, and he could smile and laugh again.

“I look back on those months of darkness and pain and remember the times I nearly walked away.

“Had he not taken the unbelievably brave step to seek help when he did, we may not have survived. I am forever grateful to him for being the man I always knew him to be, for facing his demons and staying in therapy, for not letting PTSD break him.”

Despite everything, Paul looks back on the job with a lot of pride.

Paul is calling for nationwide change to the support DFIs and their families receive, arguing that if ongoing support was provided rather than just reactive, many more would be able to continue the job for longer.



He recently published a research paper on the impact of working in this field.

Staggering statistics show 20% surveyed reported thoughts of being better off dead or of hurting themselves at a clinically significant frequency, 13% on several days, 5% more than half the days and 2% nearly every day.

And within six months, 17% considered it was likely they would leave their role, which rises to 28% at 12 months.

Paul says: “I have seen hundreds of investigators walk into the lab and some last hours, some days, some weeks because they couldn’t deal with what we dealt with on a daily basis.”

Fiona adds: “How can these DFIs be working in an environment where you are exposed to literally the worst stuff you can possibly imagine and not have preventative psychological support?

“If it had been there, then maybe Paul wouldn’t have broken. Police forces do have trauma teams, but because the DFIs are not physically on a crime scene, they are not deemed to be exposed to trauma.”

Paul, who now works as a higher assistant psychologist in the NHS, adds: “I will never be able to unsee what I’ve been exposed to, certain cases become so imprinted on you.

“You continue to wonder how the child is, how they have been affected mentally and physically, how their life is going to turn out. But I continue to heal.”

Paul now spends many hours of his own time researching and trying to raise awareness of the challenges involved with this type of role.



“I know what it did to me and if I can stop that from happening to just one other person, I’ll have achieved what I set out to do. The human cost is too great to sit back .”

Northumbria Police were approached for comment.

News.title: Aria Thorpe’s grieving dad slams ‘robbery of justice’ after daughter’s teen killer walks free from court
News.content:
THE dad of tragic nine-year-old schoolgirl Aria Thorpe has spoken for the first time since the teen who stabbed her to death walked free.

Tom Thorpe told The Sun life without his daughter – who died from a single knife wound that was deemed an accident by a jury – is “incomprehensible” and “beyond heartbreaking”.





A 16-year-old boy – who cannot be identified for legal reasons – was found not guilty of murder and manslaughter at court on Thursday (June 25).

Aria died at her home in Weston-super-Mare, North Somerset, on December 15 last year.

The boy claimed he had accidentally plunged the knife into the schoolgirl’s chest while he was jabbing it towards her in a “fencing” motion to scare her.

He said he did not intend for the blade to go into Aria.

Tom, 36, from Portsmouth, who is separated from Aria’s mum Victoria Hull, said: “We feel that the trial was a robbery of justice.

“We don’t understand how you can stand up in court, admit to stabbing Aria, claiming she wasn’t to blame, it was me 100%, but walk out the court a free man.”



He added that he is considering appealing the decision.

Tom said: “We are looking to obtain the official Crown Court transcripts with the aim to instruct an experienced, criminal appeals barrister to conduct a thorough and impartial review of the proceedings.

“This isn’t about undermining the justice system, it is about ensuring that every aspect of the trial was conducted fairly and correctly.”



He added: “How do we tell our two eldest children, who are 14 and 11, who know right from wrong, that Aria has been killed and the boy who killed her got away with it?

“We can’t get our heads around any of it. What example does this set to children across the country?”

Describing Aria, Tom went on to say: “Aria was a typical nine-year-old girl who was full of energy, curiosity, innocence and happiness.



“She loved spending time out as a family, trips to the farm, walks in the woods and playing with slime and anything messy.

“She had a real care for others, always asking how others were and wanted everyone to be happy.”

Tom continued: “Aria and her elder sister loved coming down to our house on the weekends that we had them, where they could be themselves just as the children that they were.”



He said when his eldest child comes to stay with him and partner Sophie, 34, and Aria isn’t there “the excruciating reality dawns on us all”.



He added that his toddler daughter “walks around the house asking where she is, goes upstairs to wake her up in the morning and when she isn’t in her bed she asks ‘mummy, daddy, where’s Aria gone?’”

Tom recalled his favourite memory was taking the four children to Disneyland Paris in July 2024.

He said: “We woke them up, asked what they would like to do today, they gave a few answers like going to a play area, swimming, seeing some horses, going to the beach etcetera, and then we said ‘we have an idea, shall we go Disneyland?’ and pulled out four pairs of Mickey Mouse ears.

“At first, they didn’t believe us and then we started packing the car and said ‘quick, we have 30 minutes until we leave’.

“They all ran around like it was the Home Alone house. It was magical. Aria’s face when she saw all of the princess characters, horse carriages, Moana and rides was a memory we will never forget.”



Tom said “life without Aria is incomprehensible”, adding: “This is beyond heartbreaking.”

It comes after Aria’s aunt Katie Thorpe said outside the court after the verdict: “Our family has effectively been handed a life sentence.

“We will carry this grief, heartbreak and loss for the rest of our lives. Meanwhile, the person responsible walks free.”

Bristol Crown Court heard the boy had fled to a nearby train station following the horror.

Footage showed the defendant telling a group of other youths he had stabbed someone.



He further told the group of youngsters: “You’ll see it on the news later.”

Giving evidence, he told the court he had picked up a knife from the kitchen of Aria’s home and went into the lounge where she was sitting on the sofa.

“Aria stood up and I was waving around the knife,” he told the jury.

“Then at some point I decided that I was going to try to make her flinch and scare her, to get a reaction.

“I leaned forward, acted like I was fencing.”



The court heard how Aria had spent the afternoon before she died at a dance class and was picked up by her mum Victoria Hull.

She ate pizza and seemed “bubbly and happy” – asking her mum if she could have the last Oreo.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Victoria added: “She said something like ‘see you after work mummy’. I replied ‘see you after work, love you’.”

Home Office pathologist Dr Amanda Jeffery found Aria died from a single stab wound, which went through her heart.

News.title: UK households that drain tinned tuna liquid down sink urged to stop
News.content:
UK households that drain tinned tuna liquid down sink urged to stop

People who pour the liquid down the sink have been warned of the unpleasant concequences

View 2 Images Draining tuna down the sink could lead to unpleasant issues with your drains (Image: Getty)

Anyone who drains liquids from tinned tuna down their sink has been urged to stop in a new warning. Although the act may seem harmless, it could lead to severe consequences not only for your kitchen drains but also for your neighbourhood sewer system.

‌



On Friday (June 26), BBC DIY SOS presenter Nick Knowles appeared on Morning Live to talk about fatbergs. These are the large, solid clogs made up of fats, oils, and greases that mix with other materials, leading to serious issues in sewer systems and drains.

‌



Fatbergs can cause serious flooding in properties, lead to raw sewage overflowing into rivers, harbour antibiotic-resistant superbugs, and result in millions of pounds spent on manual, high-pressure extraction. If you think there's a blockage near your home, the first thing you should do is contact your water company.

‌



To reduce your risk of unpleasant consequences from a fatberg, Nick Knowles warned people not to pour certain food items down toilets and sink drains. One item he pointed out was tinned tuna liquid.

"Don't pour your oils down the sink. I mean, most people know not to pour oils down your sink in the bathroom or in your kitchen now. But actually, most of us will drain a tin of tuna into the sink. With the oil that's in a tin of tuna, or maybe the fat from an air fryer, or coffee grounds, all these things, add to create a block."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



To avoid plumbing clogs and fatbergs, keep oils and fats away from your pipes. Instead, you can soak up small amounts of liquid with paper towels and throw them in the bin, pour it into a sealed jar or use it directly for cooking.

After cooking food with oil, Nick recommends letting the oil cool down completely, then scraping it into a container you're throwing away. "Like a baked bean tin or anything else that you're throwing, and put them in the bin and get rid of them that way", he said.

Other items he says people should avoid pouring down their drains include food grease, food scraps and coffee grounds. He also issued a warning to anyone with a toilet at home.

‌



View 2 Images Avoid pouring oils, greese, food scraps and coffee grounds down the sink (stock image)

He told viewers to never put cotton buds, nappies or wet wipes down the toilet. He said: "Wet wipes in particular... All the governments, England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, are going to be stopping the use of plastics in wet wipes, which will actually be a major boon in terms of stopping that happening."

Nick also shared a list of warning signs that there's likely a blockage in your drains or your neighbourhood's sewer systems. These include:

Article continues below

slow draining

odours

gurgling noises

pooling water by manholds

To give viewers an idea of just how large fatbergs can get, Nick provided some alarming size comparisons. He said: "In cities, you can go on tours and walk through the drains. A fatberg found near Terminal Five at Heathrow was the size of seven hundred suitcases, or the equivalent of five football pitches."
